Elasah
el-AY-sah
n. (a son of Shaphan who carried Jeremiah's letter to Babylon; also a priest in Ezra's day)
Hebrew El'asah, God hath made, from El, God, and asah, to do or make; named at Jeremiah 29:3 and Ezra 10:22.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Two men bear the name, and the better known of them carried one of the most consequential letters in the Old Testament. Zedekiah sent an embassy to Nebuchadnezzar, and Jeremiah used it as his post: the prophecy went “By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent unto Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon) saying” (Jeremiah 29:3). What he carried was the letter to the captives, and it overturned everything the exiles were being told by the prophets among them: build houses, plant gardens, take wives, seek the peace of the city, for the captivity would be seventy years and no sooner. The LORD addressed it “unto all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon” (Jeremiah 29:4) — caused, not merely permitted. The other Elasah is a priest of the sons of Pashur who had taken a strange wife and put her away (Ezra 10:22). The name means God hath made, and one of the two men spent a journey carrying the proof that God had made even the exile.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Elasah, a Hebrew proper name signifying God hath made; a son of Shaphan who bore Jeremiah's letter to the captives in Babylon, and a priest in Ezra's day.

expand to see more

Hebrew El'asah, God hath made or God hath done.

From El, God, compounded with asah, to do, make or work.

It occurs twice in this spelling in the Authorized Version, Jeremiah 29:3 and Ezra 10:22.

The first was a son of Shaphan, sent by Zedekiah on embassy to Babylon.

The second was of the sons of Pashur, who put away a strange wife.

Key Scripture

Jer 29:3 — "By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent unto Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon) saying,"

Jer 29:4 — "Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, unto all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon;"

Ezr 10:22 — "And of the sons of Pashur; Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethaneel, Jozabad, and Elasah."

Jer 29:7 — "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace."

Modern Corruption

Exile is read as the failure of God's promise; Jeremiah's letter says God caused it, set its term, and commanded His people to live faithfully inside it.

expand to see more

A disaster on this scale invites one of two errors: deny it will last, or conclude that God has abandoned the covenant. The prophets in Babylon took the first, promising a quick return, and Jeremiah's letter demolished them. It also refused the second. The captivity is from God's own hand, it has a fixed term, and in the meantime the captives are to build, plant, marry and pray — “And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it” (Jeremiah 29:7).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the absolute sovereignty of God over the worst that befalls His people, and the ordinary obedience He requires of them under it. Nothing in the letter is sentimental and nothing in it despairs. A man named God hath made carried it four hundred miles to people who needed to hear exactly that.
